effect_estimate.comment: All numeric results are extracted strictly from the readable manuscript prose; appended table/figure pages (PDF pp. 39–46, 48, 50) are blank/image-only in the extracted text, so exact regression standard errors and 95% CIs not printed in the prose are unavailable.
effect_estimate.value: In localities >=50% urbanized, household central water connections rose from 51% (1970) to 89% (2000) and full service (electricity, central water and central sewer) rose from 25% to 49%, with small migrant-type houses under-serviced relative to large houses (1980 weighted central water: 61% vs. 86%, full service: 17% vs. 54%; 1991 unweighted central water: 57% vs. 89%). In urban-area fixed-effects regressions of 1991 small-house (1–3 rooms) central water share, strategic reaction to rival localities' servicing was negative (lagged-covariate OLS beta = -0.43; spatial MLE beta = -0.53; -0.69 OLS and -0.59 MLE with equal weights), and while moving from bottom to top locality income and size quintiles increased servicing by 48 percentage points, the top-quintile income x size interaction reduced servicing by 16 percentage points (turning marginal income and scale effects negative in large, rich localities within 2–3 locality urban areas); these strategic and income x size under-servicing effects were absent under OLS for 2000 small houses (after post-1988 democratization and slum-upgrading reforms) and for 1991 large houses. In 1991–2000 locality household growth IV regressions, the 2SLS coefficient on 1991 small-house central water share was 0.74 to 0.77 (river/altitude IV = 0.78; p < 0.10, first-stage partial F ~ 13; LIML p ~ 0.05): at ~0.8, a 1 SD (0.21) reduction in water servicing reduced 10-year household growth by ~0.17 log points (mean 0.40), reducing low-educated household growth by 0.17 in 2SLS with a similarly large adverse effect on high-educated household growth; using untitled houses' central water share yielded OLS = -0.16 and imprecise LIML = 1.82 (SE = 2.22, first-stage F = 6.2). In 1980 rent hedonics, central water commanded a 12% (Sao Paulo) and 23% (Rio de Janeiro) rent premium, and central sewer commanded 9% and 18%.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 1 (Documented association). Under CODEBOOK.md §9, rating 3 is precluded because ROBINS-I overall risk of bias is at least Serious (ecological locality-level census aggregates, multiple endogenous regressors with modest first-stage partial F ~ 13 or 6.2 for untitled homes, authors explicitly note potential exclusion-restriction violations for geological/river and 1970 historical instruments, main 2SLS estimates are only marginally significant at p < 0.10, and regression tables are unrendered). Moreover, the study does not directly observe municipal utilities denying connection applications or enforcing statutory bans (authors note Brazil lacked an explicit exclusionary policy and treat the pre-late-1980s illegality of servicing informal settlements as a background presumption), instead establishing statistical and descriptive associations across locality small-house water-connection shares, land-title/tenure status, minimum lot-size zoning (>125 sq m), and rival localities' service levels.

mechanism_flags.comment: Covers pre-late-1980s legal prohibitions on providing central water/sewer to informal settlements (favelas and untitled loteamentos) and post-1988 democratization regularization/upgrading reforms, household land ownership/title and tenure status, the 1979 federal 125 sq m minimum lot-size law and stricter municipal lot-size zoning laws, spatial infrastructure planning, decentralized municipal strategic discretion in under-servicing small-house neighborhoods, and inter-municipal strategic policy competition and local/national political alignment.

study_design.comment: Pairs a spatial equilibrium model of inter-locality strategic exclusion with decennial Brazilian Census (1970, 1980, 1991, 2000) and municipal zoning survey econometrics across Minimum Comparable Areas within urban areas.
study_design.value: Quasi-experimental and spatial econometric multi-decade locality panel/cross-sectional study (instrumental variables [2SLS and LIML] cross-locality growth regressions with urban-area fixed effects, lagged-covariate OLS and spatial autoregressive/error MLE strategic-interaction regressions, and district fixed-effects hedonic rent regressions)
